result:
I've written predictions for all 50 test trials to `output/predictions.json`, and I estimate they'll be about **80% accurate** (chance is 10%).

**The problem with the data:** the labels `y` in both train and val are shifted by one class compared with the stimulus log. Every trial has `y = (movie_time_s − 1) mod 10`. For example, the segment starting at movie time 0 s is labeled 9, and the one starting at 1 s is labeled 0. `movie_time_s` matches the class definitions in `classes.json`, so I treated `y` as mislabeled and used `movie_time_s` as the true class. The shift is the same in train and val, so it can't be seen by checking one split against the other. A decoder trained on the raw `y` would have scored well on val and then been wrong on nearly every test trial.

**The decoder:** I took the square root of the spike counts, flattened each trial to 200 features (20 units × 10 bins), and used linear discriminant analysis with automatic shrinkage. I compared three models:

| Model | Cross-validated on train + val | Trained on train, scored on val |
|---|---|---|
| LDA | 0.82 | 0.87 |
| Logistic regression | 0.80 | 0.83 |
| Gaussian naive Bayes | 0.56 | 0.67 |

The final LDA was refit on train and val together.

The test trials fire slightly faster than the training trials, about 1.03 spikes per bin on average against 0.92, so I set the estimate a little below the cross-validated 0.82. The predictions are spread across all ten classes, 3 to 9 trials each.
